messages.subject: Development version numbers and ggvis scales()
messages.subject_clean: Development version numbers and ggvis scales()
messages.body_plain:
I have a few (tangentially related) questions, with varying degrees of relation to ggvis. I tend to be overly verbose, so I've used bold a little to highlight.

The first and most complete, what's going on with ggvis scales? I haven't been able to make them work in quite a while. For example (from bar-histogram.r),

ggvis(pressure,
  props = props(x ~ temperature, y ~ pressure),
  mark_rect(props(y2 = prop_const(0, scale = TRUE), width = band())),
  scales = scales(scale_ordinal("x", range = "width", padding = 0, points = FALSE))
)

returns

Error in UseMethod("component_type") :
  no applicable method for 'component_type' applied to an object of class "ggvis_scales"

I've got the bleeding edge version (pulled updates within the last couple hours) but my colleague (Aran Lunzer, also on this group) is working with a version he pulled from github at least a week ago and has not updated, and scales() is not working for him either.

In this situation, I would often provide some information to help you know exactly which versions Aran and I are running, which leads to my next question: What is your development version number philosophy? I checked out the devtools wiki (my main source for best practices in R coding, you're really providing a ton of great information) and didn't see anything there.

Only in the past year have I started doing any package development myself, and I've been relying on incrementing the version number a tiny bit and/or updating the date in my description file every time I make a "substantial" modification so I can easily verify that I have the most recent version loaded and confirm with others who are using the package. However, I've noticed that you tend to keep the version number of your package the same (e.g. 0.0.99) even as the code is updated, and you don't use the date field of the description.

I'd love to hear your philosophy on this and your recommendations for collaborative coding practices. Do you try to keep the master branch on github totally clean, so the answer to any problem is always "pull changes from github"? Is there some hidden way to tell the difference between versions people have on their local machines?

Even more tangential (but potentially related), what is the difference between what you get from install_github() and "the development version"? For example, the ggvis documentation used to say it "needs the development version of htpuv, which can't be installed with install_github." I'm currently defaulting to using git pull on ggvis and using the build and reload button in RStudio to get it running, because then I also get easy read access to the files, so this is more a curiosity question than anything else. I'm assuming you're a little ways out from a stable version, but is that the idea of install_github()? My intuition would be that install_github() would give you a version somewhere between the stability of a package on the CRAN and a totally in-development package ("the development version"?).

If this is already documented somewhere on the devtools wiki, feel free to send me a pointer. Otherwise, I think some of this material could be of interest to others and might warrant addition to the wiki.

messages.body_plain:
> The first and most complete, what's going on with ggvis scales? I haven't
> been able to make them work in quite a while. For example (from
> bar-histogram.r),
>
> ggvis(pressure,
>   props = props(x ~ temperature, y ~ pressure),
>   mark_rect(props(y2 = prop_const(0, scale = TRUE), width = band())),
>   scales = scales(scale_ordinal("x", range = "width", padding = 0, points =
> FALSE))
> )

Scales got radically simpler. You now only need

ggvis(pressure,

  props(x ~ temperature, y ~ pressure),
  mark_rect(props(y2 = prop_const(0, scale = TRUE), width = band())),

  scale_ordinal("x", range = "width", padding = 0, points = FALSE)
)

> I'd love to hear your philosophy on this and your recommendations for
> collaborative coding practices. Do you try to keep the master branch on
> github totally clean, so the answer to any problem is always "pull changes
> from github"? Is there some hidden way to tell the difference between
> versions people have on their local machines?

For now, yes, the answer is to always pull changes from github, but
this project is so bleeding edge, you should probably also be skimming
https://github.com/rstudio/ggvis/commits/master.

Currently, the development version is synonymous with install_github -
and now after some changes to shiny, you can get everything with
install_github - no need to use git from the command line. In
principle, master should always be ok, but our test coverage isn't
great yet so we may accidentally break things. The API is also still
evolving, so we will also be breaking old code on purpose.

Hadley

--

messages.body_plain:
> Thanks! That helps with my scales questions.

I've also added (very brief and not-proofread) vignettes about scales
& properties and axes & legends, so make sure to check them out too.

> For the install_github() and "development version" questions I was trying to
> ask a bit more broadly, perhaps with the possibility of adding documentation
> to the devtools wiki. In general, when do you believe in incrementing
> version numbers?

That's still an open question - my current thinking is that devtools
should probably add the git repo sha to the description (e.g.
https://github.com/hadley/devtools/issues/276) and then provide a
function to make it easy to access it.

More generally, Winston has some notes on the ggplot2 development
process that you might find helpful:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/ggplot2-release-process#releasing-a-new-version.
 For our other packages, we normally increment the version number from
(e.g) 0.6.0 to 0.6.99 to indicate that you're using a development
version.  Occasionally, we'll bump to 0.6.100 etc if another package
needs specific features and we want to make sure that users get
notified if their versions are out of sync.

> In general, what's the difference between using
> install_github() and git cloning, then building locally? If this is covered
> somewhere that I haven't run across, I'd love a pointer to the resource.

It's exactly the same.  (Unless the repo uses git-submodules in which
case install_github fails because github uses git archive to build
downloadable zipballs, and git archive doesn't know about submodules.
Joe removed the submodules from httpuv so install_github could work)

Hadley

--
Chief Scientist, RStudio

messages.body_plain:
Hi

Not sure I'm on entirely the right track, but...

After thrashing about a bit on this over a few Friday beers I discovered that the line

  needed <- setdiff(names(scale_types), names(scales))

in scales_vega.R doesn't seem to be pulling its weight.

Replacing it with the following

  needed <- setdiff(names(scale_types), lapply(scales, function(s) s$name))

hushed the complaints, allowing the texty example to work as-is and the mtcars to work with a bit of tweaking:

    ggvis(mtcars, props(y ~ mpg),
      dscale("x", "numeric", domain=c(0,500), name = "xdisp"),
      dscale("x", "numeric", domain=c(1,7), name = "xwt"),

      mark_symbol(props(x = prop(quote(disp), scale = "xdisp"))),

      mark_symbol(props(x = prop(quote(wt), scale = "xwt"), fill = "blue")),
      guide_axis("x", scale="xdisp", orient = "top", grid=FALSE),
      guide_axis("x", scale="xwt", orient = "bottom", properties = list(labels = props(fill = "blue")))
)

The domain=() seems to be needed, though in theory we should be getting vega to figure it out from the domain(s) of the dataset(s) plotted on each scale.  I've probably just failed to notice a straightforward way of enabling that.

Bye for now

Aran

We've gone with option 5:

scaled expr: x = ~mpg
scaled cnst: x = 1
scaled rctv: x = input_slider()
unscld expr: fill := ~col
unscld cnst: fill := "red"
unscld rctv: fill := input_slider()
prop obj : y = prop(...)

It's a little more verbose than before, but it's more consistent, and
really forces you to confront whether you're dealing with scaled
values or raw values.

Hadley

messages.subject: Why no faceting?
messages.body_plain: Can you speak briefly to why faceting is not likely to be supported by ggvis (except in the form of embedded plots)? Is it just going to be so easy to create multiple plots that you don't feel like it needs to be explicitly supported by the syntax, or have you had a philosophical shift away from faceted plots?

messages.subject: Re: Why no faceting?
messages.body_plain:
It's more that I think facetting is a special case of embedded plots, and will fall out naturally with just a couple of helper functions.

And embedded plots are a very natural fit to vega's group mark - I don't think implementing subplots will be hard.

Hadley
